summary: Describes how IPv6 can run over Bluetooth Low Energy, the low-power Bluetooth variant used by sensors, appliances and phones. It builds on the 6LoWPAN techniques for small devices.

eli5.summary: Tiny gadgets that use Bluetooth get a way to join the Internet and have their own addresses.

questions: how does ipv6 work over bluetooth low energy
how is the ipv6 address formed on bluetooth le
what mtu does ipv6 use over bluetooth le
subtitle: How to carry IPv6 packets over Bluetooth Low Energy links, using 6LoWPAN tricks to keep the overhead tiny.

tldr.problem: Bluetooth Low Energy devices such as sensors and appliances run on tiny batteries and send very small frames, yet they should be able to join the Internet with IPv6.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC puts an adapted 6LoWPAN layer on top of Bluetooth LE L2CAP. It uses link-local addresses built from the Bluetooth device address, a star topology with the central acting as router, optimized Neighbor Discovery and RFC 6282 header compression.
tldr.outcome: Constrained Bluetooth LE nodes can run ordinary IPv6 and upper-layer protocols such as UDP and TCP with little extra radio traffic. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and no newer RFC replaces it.

today: RFC 7668 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2015, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on RFC 6282 and RFC 6775.

sections.title: Why IPv6 Over Bluetooth LE
sections.content:
Bluetooth LE (Bluetooth Smart) is a radio technology for devices that run on very low-capacity batteries, such as a coin cell. The RFC names health monitors, environmental sensing and proximity applications as typical uses.

IPv6 suits such devices because of its large address space and its tools for stateless address autoconfiguration. This document describes how IPv6 is transported over Bluetooth LE connections using 6LoWPAN techniques. RFC 4944, RFC 6282 and RFC 6775 were written for IPv6 over IEEE 802.15.4, and Bluetooth LE links have similar characteristics, so many of those mechanisms are reused.
sections.eli5: Small battery gadgets need an Internet address, and IPv6 has plenty to go around. This RFC shows how to use it without wasting the battery.

sections.title: Bluetooth LE Basics the Design Relies On
sections.content:
Bluetooth LE moves small amounts of data infrequently at modest rates for very little energy per bit. IPv6 over Bluetooth LE depends on Bluetooth 4.1 and on the Bluetooth SIG's Internet Protocol Support Profile (IPSP) 1.0 or later. IPSP covers discovering IP-enabled devices and setting up the link-layer connection.

Two link roles matter. A central can manage several connections to peripherals, and for IPv6 the network is a star with the router usually in the central role. Direct radio communication happens only between a central and a peripheral, but two peripherals can still talk through the central using IP routing.

Every device has a 48-bit device address, either public or random. A random address has its first 46 bits randomized and the last 2 bits give the address type. Bluetooth LE does not detect address collisions, though the RFC notes that a conflict is very unlikely in a typical deployment.

The default MTU for Bluetooth LE is 27 octets, which leaves a 23-octet PDU after the 4-octet L2CAP header. To carry IPv6 packets of 1280 octets or larger, L2CAP provides fragmentation and reassembly, and IPSP negotiates a link-layer MTU of 1280 octets or higher. The MTU is negotiated separately for each direction, and an implementation that needs equal values SHALL use the smaller one.
sections.eli5: Bluetooth LE is like passing very small notes. The notes are too small for a full IPv6 letter, so the link cuts big letters into pieces and glues them back together at the other end.

sections.title: Protocol Stack and Subnet Model
sections.content:
The IPv6 stack runs in parallel to the GATT stack on top of Bluetooth LE L2CAP. GATT is needed only to discover nodes that support the Internet Protocol Support Service. UDP, TCP or any other protocol that runs over IPv6 can sit on top. Fragmentation from the 6LoWPAN standards is not used, because L2CAP already fragments.

The central normally acts as a 6LoWPAN Border Router (6LBR) and each peripheral as a 6LoWPAN Node (6LN). The 6LBR is an IPv6 router, not a link-layer switch. The RFC chooses a multilink subnet model: the whole star shares one subnet, typically one /64 prefix, while each spoke is its own link. The authors judged the cost of a separate subnet per link to be excessive for constrained nodes.

One consequence is that link-local multicast stays within a single connection, so 6LN-to-6LN traffic cannot use link-local addresses. Nodes reach each other through the shared prefix, and the 6LBR forwards the packets. The network may be connected to the Internet or be isolated, in the simplest case with one 6LBR and one 6LN.

The RFC recommends a 1280-octet MTU to avoid Path MTU discovery. IPv6 packets MUST be sent in big-endian order even though Bluetooth LE protocols such as L2CAP are little-endian.
sections.eli5: One helper sits in the middle of a star, and every gadget has its own private line to it. Gadgets cannot whisper straight to each other, so the helper passes the messages along.

sections.title: Addresses and Autoconfiguration
sections.content:
At interface start-up, both 6LN and 6LBR SHALL create a link-local address from the 48-bit Bluetooth device address used to set up the connection. A 64-bit interface identifier is made by inserting the octets 0xFF and 0xFE in the middle of the device address, with every bit copied unchanged. The identifier is then prefixed with fe80::/64. The same link-local address is used for the lifetime of the L2CAP channel, even if the device changes its random address.

Private Bluetooth device addresses are RECOMMENDED. A 6LN SHOULD pick a different address for every connection to a 6LBR, and a 6LBR SHOULD change its address periodically.

A 6LN MUST join the all-nodes multicast address but does not need the solicited-node address, because the 6LBR knows every connected device address. The 6LBR makes sure two devices with the same address are never connected at once, so duplicate address detection is done there, which saves transmissions and power. After this, the 6LN sends Router Solicitations.

For non-link-local addresses, 6LNs SHOULD NOT embed the Bluetooth device address by default. Alternatives named include Cryptographically Generated Addresses, privacy extensions, Hash-Based Addresses, DHCPv6 and static semantically opaque addresses. How a 6LBR obtains a prefix is out of scope. The 6LBR MUST set the on-link flag (L) to zero in the Prefix Information Option, so 6LNs always send packets to the 6LBR, even when the destination is another 6LN on the same prefix.
sections.eli5: Each gadget builds its first address from the serial number printed on its Bluetooth chip. For anything beyond the playroom it is encouraged to use a made-up name instead, so nobody can track it by its serial number.

sections.title: Neighbor Discovery
sections.content:
Bluetooth LE adopts only the star-topology parts of the Neighbor Discovery optimizations of RFC 6775, since mesh is not supported. A 6LN MUST NOT register its link-local address. It MUST register each non-link-local address with the 6LBR by sending a Neighbor Solicitation with an Address Registration Option (ARO) and processing the Neighbor Advertisement that comes back. This is required whichever method produced the interface identifier.

The ARO needs a 64-bit EUI-64. For Bluetooth LE it SHALL be filled with the 48-bit device address converted to Modified EUI-64 format. For Router Solicitations and Router Advertisements, 6LNs MUST follow Sections 5.3 and 5.4 of RFC 6775.

If the 6LBR finds several 6LNs with the same Bluetooth device address, or a 6LN with the 6LBR's own address, it MUST ignore the duplicates and MUST keep at most one connection for a given device address at a time.
sections.eli5: When a gadget picks a new nickname, it tells the helper in the middle. The helper keeps a list so it always knows who is who.

sections.title: Header Compression
sections.content:
Header compression as defined in RFC 6282 is REQUIRED, and all headers MUST be compressed using its encoding formats. The IPv6 payload length can be derived from the L2CAP header length, and elided addresses can be rebuilt from the link-layer address, the HCI Connection Handle, compression context and address registration information.

The 6LBR MUST include a 6LoWPAN Context Option (6CO) in each Router Advertisement for every prefix it advertises for autoconfiguration. A 6LN MUST fully elide its source address when it is link-local. For a registered non-link-local address, the source MUST be fully elided if it is the latest address registered for that prefix, using SAC=1 and SAM=11. Older addresses carry the whole 64-bit identifier in line (SAM=01) or, if the first 48 bits match the latest registered address, only the last 16 bits (SAM=10).

The 6LBR mirrors this for packets it sends. It fully elides the destination if it is the link-local address based on the 6LN's device address (DAC=0, DAM=11) or the latest address registered by the 6LN (DAC=1, DAM=11).

Registering many addresses for one compression context hurts compression: only the latest can be fully elided. An address counts as registered only after the 6LBR returns a Neighbor Advertisement with an ARO status of success.
sections.eli5: If two friends already know who is talking, they can skip saying names. The most recently introduced nickname is the one that can be dropped completely; older nicknames need a little more to be spelled out.

sections.title: Unicast and Multicast Mapping
sections.content:
The Bluetooth LE link layer does not support multicast, so traffic is always unicast between two nodes. If a 6LBR must send a multicast packet to all its 6LNs, it has to copy the packet and unicast it on every link, which may not be energy efficient, especially when the central is battery powered.

To save power, the 6LBR MUST track multicast listeners per Bluetooth LE link, not per subnet, and MUST NOT forward multicast packets to 6LNs that have not registered as listeners for the groups concerned. In the other direction, a 6LN that wants to send multicast unicasts the packet to the 6LBR.
sections.eli5: The link has no loudspeaker, only private lines. To tell everyone something, the helper has to whisper it to each gadget one at a time, and skips gadgets that did not ask to hear it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says IPv6 over Bluetooth LE and IPv6 over IEEE 802.15.4 have similar security needs. Link-layer security is covered by the IPSP. The Bluetooth LE link layer supports encryption and authentication using Counter with CBC-MAC (CCM) and a 128-bit AES block cipher, and key management is provided by the Security Manager Protocol.

On privacy, the link-local address reveals only what the 6LBR already knows from the link-layer connection. A device using Bluetooth privacy features has the same privacy at the IPv6 link-local level, and a device without them has none. That is why implementations are recommended not to embed the device address in other addresses by default.

A malicious 6LN could try to flood the network. The RFC says this is mitigated because link-local multicast is not bridged between links and because the 6LBR can rate-limit each 6LN using the L2CAP credit-based flow-control mechanism.
sections.eli5: The Bluetooth link can already lock its messages. A gadget that wears a disguise on Bluetooth keeps the disguise on the Internet too, and the helper can slow down any gadget that shouts too much.
